content.title: About
content.content: Quail eggs are small speckled eggs of the Japanese quail (Coturnix japonica). A single egg weighs about 10 grams, several times less than a chicken egg. The taste is delicate, similar to chicken egg, with a yolk that is large relative to the egg's size. The eggs are boiled, fried, and added to salads, appetizers, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: One chicken egg is roughly equal in weight to four or five quail eggs.
Quail eggshells are speckled and thin, with a tough membrane underneath.
Quail eggs take only 2–4 minutes to hard-boil.
They are often served in salads, on appetizer skewers, in soups, and in Asian dishes.
Claims that quail eggs are hypoallergenic are not scientifically supported.

items.title: Source of complete protein
items.content: The egg provides protein with all the essential amino acids.

items.title: Contain vitamin B12 and riboflavin
items.content: These vitamins support metabolism and the formation of blood cells.

items.title: Contain iron
items.content: Iron is needed for oxygen transport.

items.title: Contain selenium
items.content: Selenium is a trace mineral with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contain choline
items.content: Choline is important for nervous system function and cell membranes.

items.title: Salmonella
items.content: Raw eggs, including quail eggs, may contain Salmonella; it is best not to eat them raw, especially for children, pregnant women, older adults, and people with weakened immunity.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Egg allergy is possible, including cross-reaction with chicken eggs.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol, and people with high cholesterol should discuss how many to eat with a doctor.

items.title: Small size
items.content: Whole small eggs can be a choking hazard for small children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hard-boil quail eggs for 2–4 minutes, cool them in cold water, and peel. Add them to salads, appetizers, sandwiches, soups, and rolls and Asian dishes, or fry them whole. For safety, the white and yolk should be fully set.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggs in the refrigerator in their original package, away from strong-smelling foods, and use them before the expiration date. Do not wash them in advance. Keep boiled eggs in the refrigerator for a few days. Discard cracked eggs and eggs with an unpleasant smell.
